findings.who: A filer, or a joint filer's spouse, who gave far more than the AGI limits in 2023 or 2024 and gave nothing in 2025. They now deduct only an unused carryover on line 13.
findings.why_no: The gate asks 'In 2025, did you ... give money or things to a charity'. Nothing was given in 2025, so a truthful no sets sa.charity_limited to false. Yet the carryover is still subject to the percentage limits and may exceed them.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 11, Line 13: "Generally, the same limits apply this year to your carryover amounts as applied to those amounts in the earlier year ... After applying those limits, enter the amount of your carryover that you are allowed to deduct this year."
findings.fix: Broaden the gate: 'In 2025, did you (or your spouse) give ..., or do you have charitable gifts from 2020–2024 that you could not fully deduct (a carryover)?' Alternatively, ask the limit question whenever line 13 is non-zero, and word it to include carryovers.

findings.who: A partner or S corporation shareholder whose 2025 Schedule K-1 (box 13, code A, or box 12, code A) passes through cash contributions the entity made. The filer personally gave nothing.
findings.why_no: The words 'did you ... give money ... to a charity' describe the filer's own act. A passive investor truthfully answers no, although their share of the entity's gifts is treated as their own and belongs on Schedule A.
findings.line: sa.line11_if_gifts; also sa.charity_limited_if_gifts if the flow-through gifts are large
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 10, Line 11: "Enter on line 11 the total value of gifts you made in cash or by check". The flow-through treatment comes from the Partner's/Shareholder's Instructions for Schedule K-1, which are not in the excerpts supplied.
findings.fix: Add to the gate: '..., or does a 2025 Schedule K-1 you (or your spouse) received show charitable contributions?' Alternatively, compute the gate as true whenever a K-1 contribution entry is non-zero.

findings.who: A filer who moved cash into a donor-advised fund at a sponsor such as Fidelity Charitable or Schwab Charitable in 2025. They made no grants out of the fund that year.
findings.why_no: They think of the transfer as funding their own 'giving account' at a financial firm, not as giving money to a charity. In their view the 'charity' is whoever later receives grants from the fund.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 9: "You can deduct contributions or gifts you gave to organizations that are religious, charitable, educational, scientific, or literary in purpose"
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Count money you put into a donor-advised fund in 2025, even if the fund has not yet granted it out.'

findings.who: A filer who made a state tax-credit contribution, such as to a scholarship-granting organization or a neighborhood assistance program. The credit is less than the full payment (for example 50–70%) or 15% or less.
findings.why_no: They regard the payment as a way of paying state tax or 'redirecting' it, not as a gift to a charity, so they answer no. Part or all of the payment remains a deductible contribution.
findings.irs_text: p526 p. 5: "the amount treated as a charitable contribution deduction is reduced by the amount of the state or local tax credit"; Exception: "If the state or local tax credit ... doesn't exceed 15% of your payment amount ... your charitable contribution deduction isn't reduced."
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Count payments to a charity that earned you a state or local tax credit; the tool will remove the credited part later.'

findings.who: A filer who bought a charitable gift annuity for cash, or who paid a membership to a museum or public radio station.
findings.why_no: They see a purchase (an annuity, or a membership with perks), not a gift. The help's 'fundraising dinner' example may not suggest these payments to them.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 9: "If you made a gift and received a benefit in return ... you can generally only deduct the amount that is more than the value of the benefit"; p526 p. 5: "You may be able to deduct membership fees or dues you pay to a qualified organization."
findings.fix: Extend the help examples: 'such as a fundraising dinner, a charity auction item, a museum or public-radio membership, or a charitable gift annuity'.

findings.who: A foster parent with unreimbursed expenses whose child was placed by a county or state child-welfare agency, not by a nonprofit.
findings.why_no: The gate says a foster child that 'it' (the charity) placed. The filer does not consider the county agency a charity, even though the help mentions governments in a different context.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 9: "Contributions can be in cash, property, or out-of-pocket expenses you paid to do volunteer work"; "Federal, state, and local governments if the gifts are solely for public purposes."
findings.fix: Reword the gate as 'hosting a student or foster child placed with you by a charity or a government agency'.

findings.who: A filer who pays deductible home mortgage interest to a private lender or seller and receives no Form 1098, so the interest belongs on line 8b, and who used some of the loan proceeds for other purposes.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed only from line 8a. Line 8a is zero because no Form 1098 interest is entered there, so the tool skips the other-use question and treats it as false.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: 'If you paid home mortgage interest to a recipient who didn’t provide you a Form 1098, report your deductible mortgage interest on line 8b.'
findings.fix: Gate on any home mortgage interest on lines 8a, 8b, or 8c, or on having a home mortgage outstanding, not only line 8a > 0.

findings.who: A filer who was liable for and paid mortgage interest and whose share was reported on another borrower’s Form 1098, so the share goes on line 8b, and who used some proceeds for other purposes.
findings.why_no: Line 8a is zero because the Form 1098 is not the filer’s own; the gate never asks the other-use question.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: 'If the shared interest was reported on the other person’s Form 1098, report your share of the interest on line 8b'.
findings.fix: Gate on any home mortgage interest on lines 8a, 8b, or 8c, or on having a home mortgage outstanding, not only line 8a > 0.

findings.who: A filer whose only home mortgage item is points not reported on Form 1098, entered on line 8c, and who used loan proceeds for other purposes.
findings.why_no: Line 8a is zero because the points are on line 8c; the gate treats the other-use question as false.
findings.irs_text: f1040sa p. 1, line 8c: 'Points not reported to you on Form 1098'; i1040sca p. 8: 'Check the box on line 8 if you had one or more home mortgages in 2025 with an outstanding balance and you didn't use all of your home mortgage proceeds from those loans to buy, build, or substantially improve your home.'
findings.fix: Gate on any home mortgage interest or points on lines 8a, 8b, or 8c, or on having a home mortgage outstanding, not only line 8a > 0.

findings.who: A filer who has a Form 1098 home mortgage but used all the borrowed money for other purposes, so the deductible home mortgage interest properly entered on line 8a is zero.
findings.why_no: The gate is line 8a > $0. Because the other-use limit zeroes line 8a, the tool skips the question that would detect the other use and marks it false.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: 'Check the box on line 8 if you had one or more home mortgages in 2025 with an outstanding balance and you didn't use all of your home mortgage proceeds from those loans to buy, build, or substantially improve your home.' Also: 'Interest paid on home mortgage proceeds used for other purposes isn’t deductible on lines 8a or 8b.'
findings.fix: Gate on the existence of a home mortgage with nonqualifying-use potential, not on the deductible line 8a amount; ask the other-use question whenever there is an outstanding home mortgage.

findings.who: A filer with deductible home mortgage interest and other-use proceeds whose line 8a is reduced to zero by the mortgage interest credit on Form 8396, line 3.
findings.why_no: The gate uses the post-credit line 8a amount, which is zero, so the other-use question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: 'If you are claiming the mortgage interest credit ... subtract the amount shown on Form 8396, line 3, from the total deductible interest you paid on your home mortgage. Enter the result on line 8a.'
findings.fix: Use the pre-credit mortgage interest or the existence of the mortgage for the gate; do not let the Form 8396 subtraction zero out the gate.

findings.who: A filer with a home mortgage outstanding in 2025 but no interest paid or entered on line 8a, such as an interest-free family loan, who used some proceeds for other purposes.
findings.why_no: Line 8a is zero because there is no interest; the gate treats the other-use question as false even though the line 8 check box is based on an outstanding home mortgage and nonqualifying use.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: 'Check the box on line 8 if you had one or more home mortgages in 2025 with an outstanding balance and you didn't use all of your home mortgage proceeds from those loans to buy, build, or substantially improve your home.'
findings.fix: Gate on whether the filer had a home mortgage outstanding in 2025, not whether interest was paid or entered on line 8a.

findings.who: A couple who bought their house on a land contract (contract for deed). The seller keeps legal title until the last payment. The couple pays interest to the seller, who sends no Form 1098, and the couple pays the property tax.
findings.why_no: They do not hold title, so they answer no to 'own a home or other real estate'. The follow-up names only 'a loan secured by a boat, camper or mobile home, or ... a mortgage on a home in the name of another person', and a land contract is not called a mortgage.
findings.line: sa.mortgage_unreported_if_home (line 8b seller-paid interest; the refusal is missed), sa.line5b_if_home_owner
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 9, Line 8b: 'If you paid home mortgage interest to the person from whom you bought the home and that person didn't provide you a Form 1098, write that person's name...'; p. 8: 'A home mortgage is any loan that is secured by your main home or second home, regardless of how the loan is labeled'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Did you (or your spouse) own, or buy under a land contract, contract for deed or seller financing, a home or other real estate at any time in 2025?' Also add land contracts and seller financing to the interest follow-up.

findings.who: A tenant-stockholder in a housing cooperative. They own shares and a proprietary lease, not a deed. They pay interest on a co-op share loan reported on Form 1098, and their maintenance includes their share of the building's tax and interest. They may also have bought with a mortgage credit certificate and sold in 2025.
findings.why_no: They hold stock, not 'real estate', so they answer no to the first question. The follow-up lists 'boat, camper or mobile home' and a 'home in the name of another person' but never a co-op share loan.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8: 'A home can be a house, condominium, cooperative, mobile home, boat, or similar property'
findings.fix: Name co-ops in the gate: 'own a house, condominium, co-op apartment (shares in a housing cooperative), mobile home, timeshare, land or other real estate'. Add 'a loan secured by co-op shares' to the interest follow-up.

findings.who: A filer who owns a deeded timeshare used as a second home and pays interest on a loan secured by it, reported on Form 1098.
findings.why_no: A timeshare week is not thought of as 'a home or other real estate', and the follow-up's list of boats, campers and mobile homes does not mention timeshares.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8: 'A home mortgage is any loan that is secured by your main home or second home ... A home can be a house, condominium, cooperative, mobile home, boat, or similar property'
findings.fix: Include 'timeshare' in the ownership question and in the list of loans in the follow-up.

findings.who: A filer whose house is titled in their revocable living trust or a single-member LLC used only for personal purposes. They pay the property tax and the mortgage interest.
findings.why_no: Help that equates ownership with the name on the title leads them to answer that 'the trust owns it' or 'the LLC owns it', not that they own a home.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: 'Enter on line 5b the state and local taxes you paid on real estate you own that wasn't used for business'
findings.fix: Add help: 'Count a home held in your revocable trust or in a single-member LLC you own, and a home you are buying under a contract.'

findings.who: A filer who sold their home in December 2024 and paid a supplemental or delinquent property tax bill in 2025 for the period they owned it.
findings.why_no: The question asks 'At any time in 2025, did you ... own', and they did not own it in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: 'Only taxes paid in 2025 and assessed prior to 2026 can be deducted for 2025'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate: 'own real estate in 2025, or pay in 2025 any property tax or mortgage interest on real estate you owned earlier'.

findings.who: A joint filer whose spouse alone paid interest on a boat-home loan or on a mortgage on a home titled to the spouse's parent, while neither spouse owns real estate.
findings.why_no: The follow-up label reads 'Paid interest on a loan secured by ...' with no 'or your spouse', so the filer answers only for themselves.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8a: 'If you and at least one other person (other than your spouse if you file a joint return) were liable for and paid interest on a mortgage ...'
findings.fix: Word the follow-up as 'Did you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) pay interest in 2025 on ...'.

findings.who: The executor files a 2025 final joint return for a spouse who died in late 2025. The estate paid the decedent's last hospital and nursing bills in early 2026, within one year after death. Those bills exceed 7.5% of AGI.
findings.why_no: The gate asks about costs that 'you ... paid yourselves' 'In 2025'. The estate is not 'yourselves', and it paid in 2026. Both words give a truthful no. The help that mentions estates appears only with the gated question, which is never reached.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 1: 'Certain medical expenses paid out of a deceased taxpayer's estate can be claimed on the deceased taxpayer's final return. See Pub. 502 for details.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate: 'or, for a person who died, medical costs the estate paid within one year after the death.' Also state that bills charged to a credit card in 2025 count as paid in 2025.

findings.who: A retiree has AGI of $60,000, $2,000 of copays, Medicare Part B and D premiums withheld from Social Security, and qualified long-term care premiums. With the premiums, the total exceeds $4,500.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'medical and dental costs ... after anything insurance paid' as bills, not premiums, and answers no. To the fallback 'paid for health insurance with money already taxed' the filer also answers no. The premiums were withheld from benefits before receipt, and the filer believes those benefits are largely untaxed.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 1: 'you can include what you paid for: • Insurance premiums for medical and dental care, including premiums for qualified long-term care insurance contracts ... • The supplemental part of Medicare insurance (Medicare Part B). • The premiums you pay for Medicare Part D insurance.'
findings.fix: Say in the first question: 'counting health, dental, Medicare and long-term care insurance premiums you paid (including premiums taken out of Social Security), as well as bills.'

findings.who: A filer pays nursing-home and doctor bills for a parent who is not their dependent only because the parent has $5,200 or more of gross income. Another filer pays a child's orthodontist while the ex-spouse claims the child.
findings.why_no: 'the medical and dental costs you (or ... your spouse) paid yourselves' reads as costs for your own household. The rules on whose costs count appear only in the gated question's help.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 2: 'Your child whom you don't claim as a dependent because of the rules for children of divorced or separated parents. ... Any person you could have claimed as a dependent on your return except that person received $5,200 or more of gross income or filed a joint return.'
findings.fix: Add: 'including costs you paid for your dependents, for a child the other parent claims, and for a relative you support who has too much income to be your dependent.'

findings.who: A filer's costs fall in categories they do not think of as medical: mileage and parking to treatment, lodging for out-of-town care, special-education tuition on a doctor's advice, an attendant's wages and employment taxes, or medically required home modifications. Counted, these push the total past 7.5% of AGI.
findings.why_no: 'Medical and dental costs' brings to mind doctor and dentist bills, so the filer leaves these out and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 2: '• Ambulance service and other travel costs to get medical care. If you used your own car, you can include ... 21 cents a mile.'; p502 p. 12: 'You can include in medical expenses the cost (tuition, meals, and lodging) of attending a school that furnishes special education'
findings.fix: List the less obvious categories in the gate (travel and mileage, lodging, nursing or attendant care, special schooling, long-term care services). Or ask the line 1 amount whenever the filer itemizes and compute the 7.5% test.

findings.who: A Marketplace enrollee paid low monthly premiums because of large advance credit payments. The enrollee must repay excess APTC on Form 8962, and that repaid portion counts as premiums. With it, the total exceeds 7.5% of AGI.
findings.why_no: The filer counts only what was paid out of pocket during 2025, as 'In 2025 ... paid' suggests. The repayment made with the return feels like tax, not a medical cost.
findings.irs_text: p502 p. 12: 'any amount of advance payments of the premium tax credit that you did have to pay back can be included in medical expenses'; 'You are treated as paying $5,100 ($8,700 less the allowed premium tax credit of $3,600)'
findings.fix: For anyone with a Form 1095-A, compute the premium amount from Form 8962 instead of relying on the filer's comparison, or always ask line 1 when a 1095-A is present.

findings.who: In 2025 a filer received an insurance reimbursement for 2024 bills and also paid 2025 bills above 7.5% of AGI.
findings.why_no: 'after anything insurance paid' invites subtracting every reimbursement received in 2025. Netting the prior-year reimbursement drops the total below the threshold.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 2: 'If you received a reimbursement in 2025 for prior year medical or dental expenses, don't reduce your 2025 expenses by this amount.'
findings.fix: Change the gate to 'after insurance paid or reimbursed you for 2025 costs (do not subtract repayments of earlier years' costs).'

findings.who: A self-employed filer has low net profit, so the self-employed health insurance deduction cannot absorb all premiums. The unabsorbed premiums plus bills exceed 7.5% of AGI.
findings.why_no: The filer leaves out premiums from the first question because 'those go on my business deduction'. The filer answers no to 'money already taxed' because they consider business-deducted premiums pre-tax.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 2: 'if you claimed the self-employed health insurance deduction on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 17, reduce the premiums by the amount on line 17.'
findings.fix: Compute the unabsorbed premium excess from the self-employed health insurance worksheet and open the gate whenever it is non-zero.

findings.who: A filer near the threshold has large adjustments, or income the filer does not count, so the filer's own estimate of AGI is wrong.
findings.why_no: The filer must compute 7.5% of an AGI the return has not yet produced. A filer using gross pay instead of AGI wrongly concludes costs are under 7.5%.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 1: 'You can deduct only the part of your medical and dental expenses that exceeds 7.5% of the amount of your adjusted gross income on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 11b.'
findings.fix: Do not ask the filer to apply the threshold. Ask 'Did you pay any medical, dental or health insurance costs?', then take the amount and compare it with 7.5% of the computed AGI.

findings.who: A married filer filing separately whose spouse has not filed or decided yet, or whose spouse first filed with the standard deduction and later amends to itemize. This concerns the gated question, not the computed gate, which matches line 12b exactly.
findings.why_no: The present tense 'Is your husband or wife itemizing' invites a no when the spouse has not yet chosen. 'Ask them if you do not know' does not say the answer must match the spouse's final return.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 33, Line 12b: "If your filing status is married filing separately and your spouse itemizes deductions on their return, check the box on line 12b"; p. 34: "your standard deduction is zero"
findings.fix: Ask 'Will your husband or wife itemize deductions on their 2025 return (including an amended return)?' Add to the help: 'If they have not decided, you must agree. If one of you itemizes, the other must too. If they later amend to itemize, you must amend as well.'

locators: , State and Local Tax Deduction Worksheet, "(half the amount on line 9 if married filing separately)"

findings.who: A married-filing-separately filer who itemizes and owns a home with the spouse as tenants by the entirety. The home was damaged in a federally declared disaster in 2025, and the filer entered the full casualty loss.
findings.why_no: The question asks only whether an amount was 'paid from an account you hold with your husband or wife'. A casualty loss is not a payment from any account, so the filer truthfully answers no.
findings.line: sa.mfs_joint_paid_if_itemizing (the refusal is missed, and the full loss is deducted instead of half)
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 5, Table 1: casualty loss 'resulting from a federally declared disaster on a home you own as tenants by the entirety' → 'half of the loss, subject to the deduction limits. Neither spouse may report the total casualty loss.'
findings.fix: Add a clause: 'or does any casualty or theft loss you entered involve property you own together with your husband or wife?'

findings.who: A spouse who separated during 2025. Medical bills were paid early in 2025 from a joint checking account that was closed before the return was prepared.
findings.why_no: The question uses the present tense, 'an account you hold with your husband or wife'. On the day of the interview the filer holds no joint account, so the answer is no.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 5, Table 1: medical expenses 'paid with funds deposited in a joint checking account in which you and your spouse have an equal interest' → 'half of the total medical expenses ... unless you can show that you alone paid the expenses'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Was any amount you entered paid from an account you held, at the time of payment, with your husband or wife (even if it is now closed)?'

findings.who: A couple filing separate 2025 state returns who paid the balance due on their joint 2024 state income tax return in April 2025. The filer deducts that payment as 2025 state income tax.
findings.why_no: The question asks only about 'a joint 2025 state income tax return'. They do not file one, so the answer is no, but a 2025 state tax deduction includes a payment toward a joint return for an earlier year.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 5, Table 1: state income tax where you 'file a joint state income tax return and you're liable for only your own share of state income tax' → 'the smaller of ... the state income tax you alone paid ... or the total state income tax you and your spouse paid ... multiplied by' a gross-income fraction
findings.fix: Ask: 'or did you pay in 2025 any state or local income tax (withholding, estimates, or a balance due) for a year in which the two of you filed or will file a joint state or local return?'

findings.who: A married-filing-separately itemizer in a community property state such as California or Texas. Deductible expenses were paid from a checking account in the filer's name alone, funded with community wages.
findings.why_no: The account is not one the filer holds 'with your husband or wife', so the truthful answer is no. Under community property rules, the money and the expenses are still shared.
findings.line: sa.mfs_joint_paid_if_itemizing (a refusal is missed for an allocation the tool does not apply)
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 5, Table 1 caption: 'Caution: If you live in a community property state, these rules don't apply. See Community Property.'
findings.fix: Ask about the money, not who holds the account: 'or do you live in a community property state (AZ, CA, ID, LA, NV, NM, TX, WA, WI) or were any expenses paid with money that belongs to both of you?' Or gate community property filers out earlier.

findings.who: A married-filing-separately itemizer who paid medical bills or charitable gifts with a joint credit card, cash from a shared household fund, or a joint HSA-like or brokerage cash account.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'account' as a bank checking or savings account and does not think of a credit card or a cash pool as an account held with the spouse.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 1: 'If you and your spouse paid expenses jointly and are filing separate returns for 2025, see Pub. 504 to figure the portion of joint expenses that you can claim'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Was any amount you entered paid with money or credit you share with your husband or wife (a joint bank account, joint credit card, or shared cash)?'

findings.who: A couple who file one state return with both spouses on it but compute separate tax, as a state 'combined' return or as 'married filing separately on the same return' (for example in Iowa or Delaware). Another case is a couple who file a joint city or local income tax return.
findings.why_no: The filer does not regard a combined or same-form return as a 'joint' return, and reads 'state income tax return' as excluding a local income tax return.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 5, Table 1: state income tax where you 'file a joint state income tax return' → allocation by the gross-income fraction
findings.fix: Ask: 'or do the two of you file a single state or local income tax return together (joint, combined, or both of you on the same form)?'

findings.who: A married-filing-separately itemizer whose own medical bills or property tax were paid by the spouse from the spouse's own account. The filer entered those amounts as their own.
findings.why_no: No account is held with the spouse, so the answer is no. The help text says 'you deduct what you alone paid', but it does not prompt the filer to remove amounts the spouse paid alone.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 5, Table 1: property tax and mortgage interest on property held as tenants by the entirety → 'the property tax you alone paid' / 'the mortgage interest you alone paid'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Enter only amounts paid from your own money; leave out anything your husband or wife paid from their own account.'

locators: p. 1, "If you and your spouse paid expenses jointly and are filing separate returns for 2025, see Pub. 504 to figure the portion of joint expenses that you can claim as itemized deductions"; , Table 1, medical expenses "paid with funds deposited in a joint checking account in which you and your spouse have an equal interest", "half of the total medical expenses, subject to certain limits, unless you can show that you alone paid the expenses"; , Table 1, state income tax, "file a joint state income tax return and you’re liable for only your own share of state income tax"
p. 1, "If you and your spouse paid expenses jointly and are filing separate returns for 2025, see Pub. 504"

findings.who: A married-filing-separately filer whose spouse had no 2025 income, filed no 2025 return, and was born before January 2, 1961 or blind, but who itemized deductions on a separate 2024 return.
findings.why_no: The gate/helper says only 'spouse itemizing' without a year; the filer reads it as asking about the last return they know about and answers that the spouse itemized, so the computed condition is false and the gated question is skipped.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 33, Line 12d: 'you can check the appropriate box(es) on line 12d if your spouse had no income, isn't filing a return, and can't be claimed as a dependent'; p. 34, Exception 2 applies when 'your spouse itemizes deductions on their return'.
findings.fix: Add 'for 2025' to the gate/helper and ask whether the spouse filed a 2025 separate return with Schedule A itemized deductions; only a 2025 itemizing return should make the gate false.

locators: p. 33, Line 12d, "If your filing status is married filing separately and your spouse was born before January 2, 1961, or was blind at the end of 2025, you can check the appropriate box(es) on line 12d if your spouse had no income, isn't filing a return, and can't be claimed as a dependent on another person's return"; p. 34, Exception 2—Spouse itemizes on a separate return, "your standard deduction is zero, even if you were born before January 2, 1961, or were blind"

p. 33, Line 12d, "you can check the appropriate box(es) on line 12d if your spouse had no income, isn't filing a return, and can't be claimed as a dependent on another person's return"; p. 34, Exception 2—Spouse itemizes on a separate return, "your standard deduction is zero, even if you were born before January 2, 1961, or were blind"
p. 34, Exception 2—Spouse itemizes on a separate return, "your standard deduction is zero, even if you were born before January 2, 1961, or were blind"

findings.who: A married-filing-separately filer whose only mortgage interest goes on line 8b, not line 8a. Examples are seller-financed debt with no Form 1098, or interest on a loan shared with someone whose name is on the Form 1098. The mortgage debt is over $375,000.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed as 'Home mortgage interest is entered on line 8a' and MFS, so it is false. The question is never asked and the line is set to no, even though the debt limit applies equally to interest on line 8b.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8b: "report your deductible mortgage interest on line 8b. Your deductible mortgage interest may be less than what you paid if one or more of the limits on home mortgage interest apply to you"; Shared interest: "If the shared interest was reported on the other person's Form 1098, report your share of the interest on line 8b"
findings.fix: Compute the gate as home mortgage interest (or points) entered on line 8a, 8b, or 8c, and married filing separately. Do not base it on line 8a alone.

findings.who: An MFS filer with a $300,000 mortgage on the house who also owes $100,000 on a boat, motor home, or mobile home with sleeping, toilet, and cooking facilities that serves as a second home. Or a filer whose only home is a cooperative apartment financed by a share loan.
findings.why_no: The question asks about 'the loans on your home' and the help says 'a second home'. A filer reads 'home' as a house or condo. They do not count a boat or RV loan, or a co-op share loan secured by stock, so they total $300,000 and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8: "A home can be a house, condominium, cooperative, mobile home, boat, or similar property. It must provide basic living accommodations including sleeping space, toilet, and cooking facilities."
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Count every loan secured by your main home or a second home. A home can be a house, condo, co-op, mobile home, boat, or RV with sleeping, toilet, and cooking facilities.'

findings.who: An MFS filer with a $300,000 first mortgage and a $90,000 home equity line of credit, or a 'personal' or 'business' loan secured by the house.
findings.why_no: The filer thinks of 'the loans on your home' as the mortgage only. They leave out a HELOC, or a loan the lender labeled as something other than a mortgage, and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8: "A home mortgage is any loan that is secured by your main home or second home, regardless of how the loan is labeled. It includes first and second mortgages, home equity loans, and refinanced mortgages."
findings.fix: Reword the question: 'Did all loans secured by your homes, including second mortgages, home equity loans and lines of credit, however labeled, add up to more than $375,000 at any time in 2025, or to more than the home is worth?'

findings.who: An MFS filer with two homes. A second home worth $150,000 carries $180,000 of loans, and the main home has ample equity. The total debt is under $375,000.
findings.why_no: The question says 'more than the home is worth', in the singular. The filer compares total loans with the combined value of both homes, or with the main home only, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Limit when loans exceed the fair market value of the home: "If the total amount of all mortgages is more than the fair market value of the home, see Pub. 936"
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Check each home on its own: are the loans on that home more than that home is worth?'

locators: p. 8, Limits on home mortgage interest, "deduct home mortgage interest on up to $750,000 ($375,000 if you are married filing separately) of that debt"

p. 8, Limits on home mortgage interest, "you can only deduct home mortgage interest on up to $1,000,000 ($500,000 if you are married filing separately) of that debt", "deduct home mortgage interest on up to $750,000 ($375,000 if you are married filing separately) of that debt", "If the total amount of all mortgages is more than the fair market value of the home"

findings.who: A married couple filing separately. One spouse paid interest, reported on Form 1098, on a $500,000 mortgage on their main home.
findings.why_no: The gate is false for every married-filing-separately return, so the question is never asked. The gated line is set to no even though the separate-return limits ($375,000, or $500,000 for older debt) are the lowest of all.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "you can only deduct home mortgage interest on up to $750,000 ($375,000 if you are married filing separately) of that debt"; "$1,000,000 ($500,000 if you are married filing separately)"
findings.fix: Ask every return with home mortgage interest. Compare the debt with $375,000 / $500,000 for married filing separately and $750,000 / $1,000,000 otherwise, or refuse every separate return that has home mortgage interest.

findings.who: A filer whose only home mortgage interest goes on line 8b: a $900,000 seller-financed note with no Form 1098, or a co-borrower's share shown on someone else's Form 1098, or a co-op tenant-stockholder's share of interest that was not on a 1098.
findings.why_no: The gate requires interest entered on line 8a, which holds only Form 1098 amounts. With nothing on 8a the gate is false and the debt limit is never tested.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8b: "Your deductible mortgage interest may be less than what you paid if one or more of the limits on home mortgage interest apply to you."
findings.fix: Make the gate true when home mortgage interest is entered on line 8a or line 8b (and line 8c points), not only line 8a.

findings.who: A joint return. The filer's main home has a $600,000 mortgage, and the spouse alone holds a $250,000 mortgage on a vacation condo, or brought that mortgage into the marriage.
findings.why_no: The question says "the loans on your home". The filer counts only their own home and loans and answers no, although the joint limit applies to the combined debt.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "A home mortgage is any loan that is secured by your main home or second home"; "deduct home mortgage interest on up to $750,000 ... of that debt"
findings.fix: "Did the loans on your or your spouse's main home and second home, all added together, come to more than $750,000 at any time in 2025?"

findings.who: A filer with a $700,000 house mortgage and a $120,000 loan on a liveaboard boat, RV or mobile home that has sleeping, toilet and cooking facilities and is used as a second home.
findings.why_no: "Loans on your home" and "a second home" read as houses. The filer does not count the boat or RV loan as a home loan, so the total seems to stay under $750,000.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "A home can be a house, condominium, cooperative, mobile home, boat, or similar property. It must provide basic living accommodations including sleeping space, toilet, and cooking facilities."
findings.fix: Add to the help: "A second home can be a boat, RV, mobile home, condo or co-op with sleeping, toilet and cooking facilities. Count home equity loans and lines of credit too."

findings.who: A filer with a main home worth well above its loans and a second home whose $300,000 loan is more than its $250,000 value, or a filer who compares the loan with the purchase price or the tax assessment instead of today's market value.
findings.why_no: "More than the home is worth" uses the singular and gives no measure of worth. The filer nets both homes together, or uses the purchase price or assessed value, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "If the total amount of all mortgages is more than the fair market value of the home, see Pub. 936 to figure your deduction."
findings.fix: "Were the loans on either home, counted home by home, more than that home's market value (what it would sell for, not what you paid or its assessed value) at any time in 2025?"

findings.who: A filer whose $900,000 loan was taken out in 2016 and refinanced in 2020 at a higher balance, or who has some debt from before December 15, 2017 and some from after.
findings.why_no: The help says the limit is $1,000,000 "if all of it was borrowed on or before December 15, 2017." The filer may treat the refinance as a pre-2017 loan, use the $1,000,000 limit, and answer no, although the extra amount borrowed in the refinance is new debt under the $750,000 limit.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "the $750,000 limit for debt taken out after December 15, 2017, is reduced by the amount of your qualifying debt subject to the $1,000,000 limit"
findings.fix: Add to the help: "A refinance counts as borrowed before December 15, 2017 only up to the balance it replaced. If any loan was taken out or increased after that date, use $750,000."

locators: p. 8, Limits on home mortgage interest, "deduct home mortgage interest on up to $750,000 ($375,000 if you are married filing separately) of that debt"

p. 8, Limits on home mortgage interest, "you can only deduct home mortgage interest on up to $1,000,000", "deduct home mortgage interest on up to $750,000", "If the total amount of all mortgages is more than the fair market value of the home"
Schedule A (2025), lines 1–18

findings.who: A filer who paid a yearly personal property tax to a U.S. territory, such as Puerto Rico, on a car or other property.
findings.why_no: The main gate help says a U.S. territory's tax counts, so they answer Yes. The follow-up helper asks only whether they paid a 'state or local tax'; a territory tax is not a state or local tax, so they truthfully answer No and the line is zeroed.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3: 'Include taxes imposed by a U.S. territory with your state and local taxes on lines 5a, 5b, and 5c.'
findings.fix: Make the follow-up say 'state, local, or U.S. territory tax' or remove the redundant follow-up and use the main gate.

findings.who: A filer whose yearly car registration charge is partly based on the car's value and partly on weight or a flat amount.
findings.why_no: The main help says any part based on value is Yes, but the follow-up helper asks whether the tax is 'based on the value of the property' without saying 'any part'; the filer reads that as requiring the whole charge to be value-based and answers No.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6: 'You can deduct only the part of the fee that was based on the car's value.'
findings.fix: Use 'any part of the charge was based on value' in the follow-up, as the main help does.

findings.who: A filer who paid a yearly value-based personal property tax on property other than a car or boat, such as a mobile home, aircraft, or other tangible personal property.
findings.why_no: The follow-up helper gives only 'such as a car or a boat' and omits the main gate's 'other belongings'; the filer reads the list as limited to cars and boats and answers No.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6: 'Enter on line 5c the state and local personal property taxes you paid, but only if the taxes were based on value alone and were imposed on a yearly basis.'
findings.fix: Say 'personal property, such as a car, boat, or other belongings' in the follow-up.

findings.who: A filer who in 2025 paid a personal property tax bill that was for 2024 or another prior year and was assessed before 2026.
findings.why_no: They read 'In 2025' as asking about a 2025 tax year bill, not about a payment made in 2025 for an earlier year's bill, and answer No.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 7: 'Only taxes paid in 2025 and assessed prior to 2026 can be deducted for 2025.'
findings.fix: Add 'including a prior year's bill paid in 2025' or ask about payments made during 2025.

findings.who: A filer who sold or disposed of the car or boat before 2025 but paid a delinquent personal property tax bill on it in 2025.
findings.why_no: They read 'on a car, a boat' as requiring current ownership and answer No because they no longer own the property.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 7: 'Only taxes paid in 2025 and assessed prior to 2026 can be deducted for 2025.'
findings.fix: Say 'even if you no longer own the property' or ask about tax paid on property you formerly owned.

findings.who: A filer who paid a U.S. territory personal property tax that is partly allocable to excluded income and partly not.
findings.why_no: They read the gated question's help 'unless it belongs to income left out of this return' as excluding the whole territory tax and answer No, missing the non-excluded part.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3: 'However, don't include any U.S. territory taxes you paid that are allocable to excluded income.'
findings.fix: Clarify that only the allocable excluded part is omitted; answer Yes if any part is not allocable to excluded income.

locators: Schedule A (2025), lines 1–18

p. 3, U.S. territory taxes, "Include taxes imposed by a U.S. territory with your state and local taxes on lines 5a, 5b, and 5c", "However, don't include any U.S. territory taxes you paid that are allocable to excluded income"; p. 6, Line 5c, "Enter on line 5c the state and local personal property taxes you paid, but only if the taxes were based on value alone and were imposed on a yearly basis", "You can deduct only the part of the fee that was based on the car's value"; p. 7, "Only taxes paid in 2025 and assessed prior to 2026 can be deducted for 2025"

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly where only the spouse holds title to real estate, for example a foreign condo or a house with a sidewalk-construction assessment on its bill, and that property's tax is in the real estate tax amount the return carries (for example from Form 1098 box 10 or the spouse's entry).
findings.why_no: The parent helper says "You owned a home or other real estate, or paid interest on a loan secured by a home". The filer owns nothing and pays no mortgage, so they truthfully answer no, and the nondeductible-amount question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: "Don't include the following amounts on line 5b. • Foreign taxes you paid on real estate. • ... Charges for improvements that tend to increase the value of your property"
findings.fix: Word the parent gate as "You or your spouse owned a home or other real estate (now or at any time in 2025), or paid interest on a loan secured by a home". Also make every source of the real estate tax amount open the leave-out question, not ownership alone.

findings.who: A homeowner who paid a $6,000 2025 tax bill and later in 2025 received a $400 rebate or abatement of that 2025 tax. They entered the $6,000 they paid.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether the amount entered "include[s] ... a refund or rebate of 2025 tax". The $6,000 is money paid out and contains no refund, so the filer answers no. The refund is a separate receipt that IRS text subtracts, not a part of the entered amount.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Refunds and rebates: "If you received a refund or rebate in 2025 of real estate taxes you paid in 2025, reduce your deduction by the amount of the refund or rebate."
findings.fix: Ask separately: "Did you or your spouse get back any 2025 real estate tax in 2025 (a refund, rebate, abatement credit, or an amount the buyer paid you for taxes at a sale)?" Then subtract that amount whatever the entered amount contains.

findings.who: A filer who sold a home in 2025 after paying that year's full tax bill. At closing the buyer was charged the post-sale share, shown on the settlement statement and in box 6 of Form 1099-S. The filer entered the bills they paid from bank records.
findings.why_no: "Tax charged to the buyer on a sale" reads as tax the buyer paid, which is not in the seller's figure, so the seller answers no. IRS text treats that amount as a refund that reduces the seller's deduction even though the seller's entered amount is wholly their own payments.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: "If you sold your home in 2025, any real estate tax charged to the buyer should be shown on your settlement statement and in box 6 of any Form 1099-S you received. This amount is considered a refund of real estate taxes."
findings.fix: Ask directly: "Did you or your spouse sell real estate in 2025? Enter any real estate tax charged to the buyer (settlement statement, Form 1099-S box 6)." Subtract it without regard to whether the filer thinks the entered amount 'includes' it.

findings.who: A homeowner who entered the amount on their 2025 tax bill, which they actually paid in January or February 2026, or who entered escrow deposits rather than what the lender disbursed to the taxing authority in 2025.
findings.why_no: The list names only "tax not assessed before 2026". This tax was assessed in 2025, so none of the listed items applies and the filer answers no, though it was not paid in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6: "Only taxes paid in 2025 and assessed prior to 2026 can be deducted for 2025." and "If your mortgage payments include your real estate taxes, you can include only the amount the mortgage company actually paid to the taxing authority in 2025."
findings.fix: Add to the list: "tax not actually paid in 2025 (a 2025 bill paid in 2026, or escrow deposits the lender did not pay to the taxing authority in 2025)". Or state at entry that only amounts paid to the taxing authority during 2025 count.

findings.who: A filer whose entered real estate tax includes tax on property used in a business (a home office share or a separate shop), tax on property they do not own (paying a parent's or child's bill), or a levy not assessed uniformly or not used for general purposes (a special district or HOA-type charge billed with the tax).
findings.why_no: The question lists six kinds of nondeductible amount after a colon. The filer reads the list as complete and answers no because none of these situations appears on it.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: "Enter on line 5b the state and local taxes you paid on real estate you own that wasn't used for business, but only if the taxes are assessed uniformly at a like rate on all real property throughout the community, and the proceeds are used for general community or governmental purposes."
findings.fix: Extend the list with "tax on real estate used in a business, tax on real estate you and your spouse don't own, or a charge not assessed at a like rate on all property in the community", and say "for example" before the list so it is not read as complete.

findings.who: A tenant-stockholder in a cooperative, or a buyer under a land contract or a life tenant, who pays real estate tax but does not hold title.
findings.why_no: The parent asks whether they "owned a home or other real estate". A co-op holder owns stock and a contract buyer has no deed, so either may answer no. The leave-out question is then skipped for any amount entered elsewhere (for example a co-op's share of taxes).
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: "Enter on line 5b the state and local taxes you paid on real estate you own ... Pub. 530 explains the deductions homeowners can take."
findings.fix: Add help to the parent: "Count a co-op apartment, a home bought under a land contract, and a life estate."

locators: p. 6, Line 5b, "Don't include the following amounts on line 5b", "Foreign taxes you paid on real estate"
p. 6, Line 5b, "Don't include the following amounts on line 5b", "Itemized charges for services to specific property or persons"
Schedule A (2025), lines 1–18

findings.who: A retiree or other filer with no wages whose state income tax was withheld only from a pension or IRA distribution (Form 1099-R), unemployment benefits (Form 1099-G), gambling winnings (Form W-2G), or contractor pay (Form 1099-NEC/1099-MISC).
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether state or local tax was 'taken out of your ... pay' and points to Form W-2 boxes 17 and 19. A pension, an unemployment check, or a jackpot is not 'pay', and they have no W-2, so the truthful answer is no. Even after a yes, the gated question adds only W-2 boxes 17 and 19.
findings.line: sa.line5a_if_state_tax (and through it Schedule A line 5a), unless another input captures non-W-2 withholding
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: "State and local income taxes withheld from your salary during 2025. Your Form(s) W-2 will show these amounts. Forms W-2G, 1099-G, 1099-R, 1099-MISC, and 1099-NEC may also show state and local income taxes withheld"
findings.fix: Broaden the gate: 'In 2025, was state or local income tax withheld from any payment to you (or, on a joint return, your spouse), such as pay (Form W-2 boxes 17 and 19), a pension or IRA distribution (Form 1099-R), unemployment benefits (Form 1099-G), gambling winnings (Form W-2G), or nonemployee pay (Form 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC)?' Ask for each form's state and local withholding box. Keep the exclusion for tax deducted on Schedule C, E, or F. If a separate input already collects non-W-2 withholding, say so in this help text.

findings.who: An employee in California, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island or Washington whose pay had mandatory state disability, family leave, or unemployment fund contributions withheld (often shown in W-2 box 14 as SDI, FLI, DBL, or UI/WF/SWF), but no state income tax.
findings.why_no: These contributions are not 'income tax' and are not in boxes 17 or 19, so the filer answers no. That is correct for this line, but if the tool has no other input for these contributions, the 5a amount is lost.
findings.line: Schedule A line 5a component reached only through this gate (if no separate input exists for mandatory state fund contributions)
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: "Mandatory contributions you made to the California, New Jersey, or New York Nonoccupational Disability Benefit Fund ... Mandatory contributions to the Alaska, California, New Jersey, or Pennsylvania state unemployment fund. Mandatory contributions to state family leave programs"
findings.fix: Ask a separate ungated question about mandatory state disability, family leave, or unemployment fund contributions withheld from pay (often in W-2 box 14), or add to this gate's help: 'State disability (SDI), family leave (FLI), and state unemployment contributions in box 14 are asked separately.'

findings.who: A worker whose local tax is called a 'wage tax', 'earned income tax', or 'school district tax' (for example, the Philadelphia wage tax, Pennsylvania EIT, or an Ohio school district tax), or whose employer reports it in box 14 rather than box 19.
findings.why_no: The filer does not see a 'wage tax' or an amount in box 14 as 'income tax' or as box 19, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: "State and local income taxes withheld from your salary during 2025."; fw2 p. 4: "19 Local income tax"
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Include local taxes on wages, such as city wage taxes, earned income taxes, or school district income taxes, even if your employer shows them in box 14 instead of box 19.'

findings.who: A filer whose only state payment in 2025 was the balance due on the 2024 state return, paid in April 2025. Nothing was withheld from other income, and no estimates were paid for 2025.
findings.why_no: The question reads 'In 2025, did you ... pay state or local income tax not taken from pay (such as estimated payments, or a past refund applied to 2025)'. Every example concerns 2025's tax, and neither the question nor its help mentions tax paid with last year's return. The filer reads it as 'tax for 2025' and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: "State and local income taxes paid in 2025 for a prior year, such as taxes paid with your 2024 state or local income tax return."
findings.fix: Name it in the question: '... such as estimated payments, a balance paid with your 2024 state or local return, or a past refund applied to 2025'. Also add 'tax you paid in 2025 for an earlier year' to the help.

findings.who: A former freelancer who closed the business in 2024 and whose only 2025 state payment was the fourth-quarter 2024 estimate, paid in January 2025.
findings.why_no: The filer takes 'estimated payments' and 'In 2025' to mean estimates for the 2025 tax year. They regard the January payment as 2024 tax and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: "State and local estimated tax payments made during 2025"; "State and local income taxes paid in 2025 for a prior year"
findings.fix: Say 'any payment of state or local income tax made during 2025, whatever year it was for (for example, a January 2025 estimate for 2024)'.

findings.who: A California, New Jersey or New York employee, or one of a married couple, whose only qualifying amount is SDI, SUI or family leave contributions deducted from pay and shown in Form W-2 box 14. There are no estimates and no other withholding.
findings.why_no: The question opens with 'not taken from pay', and the filer applies that limit to the whole sentence. Some employees also think of the box 14 deductions as payroll items their employer handled, not money they 'paid into' a fund. The help says to count 'SDI, SUI or FLI from pay', but it conflicts with the question's opening limit.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: "Mandatory contributions you made to the California, New Jersey, or New York Nonoccupational Disability Benefit Fund ..."; "Mandatory contributions to state family leave programs"
findings.fix: Split the gate into two questions. One asks about tax not taken from pay. A separate one asks: 'Did your pay stub or Form W-2 (box 14) show SDI, SUI, FLI, PFL or a state disability, unemployment, workers' compensation or family leave deduction?'

findings.who: A filer who had state income tax withheld on something outside the help's list. Examples: nonresident withholding on the sale of real property (California Form 593), state withholding on a brokerage Form 1099-B, 1099-DIV or 1099-INT, or pass-through entity withholding reported to the filer as a nonresident partner.
findings.why_no: The help names 'a pension, IRA, unemployment pay, winnings, 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC'. The filer takes this as the complete list of withholding that counts, and treats a withheld amount on a house sale or brokerage account as not 'paid'.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: "State and local income taxes withheld ... Forms W-2G, 1099-G, 1099-R, 1099-MISC, and 1099-NEC may also show state and local income taxes withheld"
findings.fix: Make the help say 'any state or local income tax withheld from anything other than wages, such as a pension, IRA, unemployment, winnings, a property sale, a brokerage account or a partnership'.

findings.who: A partner or S corporation shareholder whose state nonresident income tax was paid on their behalf through a composite return or entity-level withholding. The filer wrote no check and had nothing withheld.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether 'you ... pay state or local income tax'. The entity paid it, so the filer truthfully says they did not pay.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: "include on line 5a the state and local income taxes listed next" (taxes withheld or paid for the individual's own liability)
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Count state income tax a partnership or S corporation paid or withheld for you as a nonresident (shown on your K-1 or state form).'

findings.who: A filer who made a cash gift to a qualifying charity for a state tax credit in 2023, then carried the unused credit forward and applied it to the 2025 state income tax.
findings.why_no: The filer did not 'pay' anything in 2025, because the credit only reduced their tax. They read 'a state tax credit for a charity gift' in a question headed 'In 2025' as a gift made in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Safe harbor: "To the extent you apply a portion of the credit to offset your state or local tax liability in a subsequent year (as permitted by law), you may treat this amount as state or local tax paid in the year the credit is applied."
findings.fix: Say 'a state or local tax credit from a charity gift (made in 2025 or earlier) that you applied to your income tax in 2025'.

findings.who: A filer with Puerto Rico, Guam or USVI wages whose territory income tax was withheld and reported on Form 499R-2/W-2PR or a territory W-2 rather than a U.S. Form W-2 with state boxes.
findings.why_no: The question says 'state or local income tax not taken from pay', so the filer answers no because the tax was taken from pay. The gated input also excludes tax 'taken out of pay'. If the wage-withholding input reads only Form W-2 box 17 and 19, the territory tax is lost.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3: "Include taxes imposed by a U.S. territory with your state and local taxes on lines 5a, 5b, and 5c."
findings.fix: Confirm that the from-pay input explicitly counts territory income tax withheld on territory wage statements. If it does not, count territory tax withheld from pay in this gate and its amount.
